questions.question: Is commutativity required for a monoid?
options: No. A monoid may be noncommutative.
No, because monoids are not associative.
Yes. Every monoid is Abelian.
Only if the set is finite.

questions.question: Why are positive integers under addition not a monoid if $0$ is excluded?
options: Positive integers are not closed under addition.
Addition is not associative.
The additive identity $0$ is not in the set.
Every positive integer has an inverse.

questions.question: On $\{0,1,2\}$ with operation $\max$, which element is the identity?
options: There is no identity.

questions.question: What can prevent a semigroup from being a monoid?
options: The absence of an identity element in the set.
The absence of inverses for some of its elements.
The absence of commutativity in its operation.
The presence of an absorbing element such as $0$.

questions.question: Is $(\mathbb{N}_0,\times)$ a monoid?
options: Yes, with identity $1$.
No, because $1$ is not in $\mathbb{N}_0$.
No, because $0$ has no inverse.
No, because multiplication is not associative.

questions.question: For $a\star b=a+b+1$ on $\mathbb{Z}$, what is the identity element showing that this is a monoid?
options: No identity exists.

questions.question: A set has a binary operation with an identity element. What else must be checked before calling it a monoid?
options: That the operation is associative.
Nothing: an identity already forces associativity.
That every element has an inverse.
That the operation is commutative.

questions.question: In a monoid with identity $e$, why is the power $a^0$ defined for every element $a$?
options: It is set equal to $e$, the value of the empty product.
Associativity alone gives the empty product a value.
Every element has an inverse, so $a^0=a\star a^{-1}$.
The operation is commutative, so factors can be removed.

questions.question: On the positive real numbers with multiplication, which structure is present?
options: Not even a semigroup.
A monoid but not a group.
A semigroup but not a monoid.
A group, and therefore also a monoid.

questions.question: For a nonempty finite set $A$, let $M_A$ be the set of all functions $f\colon A\to A$, with composition $\circ$ as the operation. $M_A$ is a monoid whose identity is the identity function $x\mapsto x$. For which sets $A$ is $M_A$ also a group?
options: For every such $A$, since the self-maps of a finite set are permutations.
Exactly when $A$ has one element.
For no such $A$, since composition is not commutative.
Exactly when $A$ has at most two elements.
